Test Case Title: Verify that one common Login screen is presented with no user-type selector
Test Case Objective / Description: Every Pacco user, administrator or ordinary, is meant to arrive at the same sign-in screen and never be asked to declare what kind of user they are. This test proves there is only one entry point and no control, link or address parameter that lets a user claim administrator status. Without it the platform could ship a second admin entry point and leak an authorisation decision to the browser.
Preconditions:
1. The Pacco browser client is running locally at http://localhost:5173.
2. No session is held in the browser.
Test Data:
Client URL = http://localhost:5173
Browser viewport = 1440x900
Probed admin addresses = http://localhost:5173/admin/login, http://localhost:5173/login?role=admin

Automation hint: render the login route, assert exactly one form, assert no element whose accessible name or value matches /admin|administrator|user type|role/i, and assert /admin/login resolves to the same login screen.
Test Steps:
1. Open http://localhost:5173/ in a Chromium browser sized 1440x900.
2. Read every visible control on the screen.
3. Open http://localhost:5173/admin/login in the same browser.
4. Open http://localhost:5173/login?role=admin in the same browser.
5. Inspect the rendered markup for any hidden field, toggle or option naming a user type.
Expected Result per Step:
1. The browser lands on the Login screen; the heading reads "Sign in".
2. Exactly three interactive controls are present: the "Email or Username" field, the "Password" field with its reveal control, and the "Sign in" action, plus the "Need help?" link. No user-type toggle, radio group or dropdown is present.
3. The same single Login screen renders; no separate administrator sign-in screen exists.
4. The same single Login screen renders and the address parameter changes nothing on screen.
5. No hidden input, data attribute or option value names a role, a user type or an administrator mode.
Expected Outcome: A single common Login screen serves both audiences and offers no way for a user to declare a user type.
Postconditions / Cleanup: 1. None — read-only test.
Covered Acceptance Criteria:
AC-1
Given any Pacco account, administrator or ordinary, when the user opens the application, then the same /login screen is presented, and no control, field, link or query parameter on it allows the user to declare a user type.
Traceability:
Requirement IDs: AC-1, FR-1, DO1
Jira: 13652

This test pins the heading, subheading, both field labels and both helper strings to the approved copy so no later change silently rewrites them. A regression here is how a screen drifts away from its approved design without anyone noticing.

Expected heading = Sign in

Expected identifier label = Email or Username
Expected identifier helper = Enter your email address or username.
Expected password label = Password
Expected password helper = Enter your password.
Expected link text = Need help?

Automation hint: assert each string with an exact-match text query, not a substring match.

4. The label reads exactly "Password"; the helper text reads exactly "Enter your password.".
5. The link text reads exactly "Need help?".
Expected Outcome: Every approved string on the Login screen renders character for character as specified.
Postconditions / Cleanup: 1. None — read-only test.
Covered Acceptance Criteria:
AC-1
Given any Pacco account, when the user opens the application, then the same /login screen is presented with its approved control set and copy.

Test Case Title: Verify that five rapid activations of Sign in produce exactly one request
Test Case Objective / Description: An impatient user clicking Sign in repeatedly must not create five authentication attempts, which would both confuse the result and hammer the platform. This test drives five activations inside the window of a single slow response and counts what actually left the browser. Without the lock, repeated clicking multiplies load and can leave the screen showing the outcome of the wrong attempt.
Preconditions:
1. The Pacco browser client is running locally at http://localhost:5173.
2. The sign-in endpoint is intercepted and held for 2000 ms before responding.
3. Network traffic from the browser is being recorded.
Test Data:
Client URL = http://localhost:5173/login
Identifier = jane.smith@pacco.example.com
Password = Str0ng-Passphrase!2026
Intercepted response delay = 2000 ms
Activation count = 5, spaced 100 ms apart

Automation hint: stub POST http://localhost:5000/identity/sign-in with a 2000 ms delayed 200; fire 5 click events 100 ms apart; assert exactly 1 recorded request.
Test Steps:
1. Open http://localhost:5173/login in a Chromium browser sized 1440x900, fill both fields with the test data and start recording network traffic.
2. Activate "Sign in" five times at 100 ms intervals.
3. While the response is still pending, read the state of the "Sign in" action.
4. While the response is still pending, read the state of both fields.
5. Let the response arrive, then count the recorded requests to the sign-in address.
Expected Result per Step:
1. The Login screen renders with both fields filled and the primary action enabled.

Test Case Title: Verify that a browser request from the allowed origin is accepted and echoed

Preconditions:
1. The Docker Compose backend stack is running with the gateway published on http://localhost:5000.

3. A command-line HTTP client is available to replay the captured token.

Identifier = jane.smith@pacco.example.com
Password = Str0ng-Passphrase!2026
Captured value = the access token issued by the platform before logout
Replay target = any gateway route that requires a token

contract:
  method: GET
  path: any gateway route that requires a token
  base: http://localhost:5000
  auth: the access token captured before logout
  expected_status: the same status the route returns for a valid token — the replay is expected to be accepted
  expected_result: acceptance is the recorded, accepted outcome of client-side logout; it is not a failure of this capability

Automation hint: record the observed outcome and the time remaining until the token's own expiry; never fail the pipeline on acceptance.

Identifier = jane.smith@pacco.example.com
Password = Str0ng-Passphrase!2026

Test Case Title: Verify that the session is re-checked on every navigation and never reused
Test Case Objective / Description: A guard that caches its first verdict keeps a user inside the protected screen long after the session has died. This test opens the landing screen, lets the session expire while the screen is still open, then navigates to it again. The second navigation must be decided afresh rather than inherited from the first.
Preconditions:
1. The Pacco browser client is running locally at http://localhost:5173.
2. The browser clock can be controlled by the test harness.
3. A session can be seeded directly into browser storage by the test harness.
Test Data:
Session at the first navigation = live, expiring two seconds from now
Clock advance between the two navigations = five seconds
Second navigation = the same landing address, reached from inside the running application without a full page reload
Expected = allowed on the first navigation, denied on the second

Automation hint: spy on the liveness check, assert its call count rises by one per navigation and assert the second verdict differs from the first.
Test Steps:
1. Seed a session that expires two seconds from now and open http://localhost:5173/welcome.
2. Stay on the landing screen and advance the browser clock by five seconds without reloading the page.
3. Navigate to the root address and back to the landing address from inside the running application.
4. Read the recorded calls to the liveness check across both navigations.
5. Request the landing address once more.
Expected Result per Step:
1. The session is live and the landing screen renders.
2. The screen stays exactly as it was; nothing re-renders on its own, because no background timer watches the session.
3. The second navigation is denied: the user is taken to the Login screen with the session-expired notice and no landing element appears at any point, including transiently.
4. The liveness check ran again for the second navigation; the first verdict was not reused and no cached answer was returned.
5. The address is denied again with the same verdict, so the deny is stable rather than a one-off.
Expected Outcome: Every navigation to the protected screen is decided by a fresh liveness check, so a session that dies while the screen is open is caught on the very next navigation.
Postconditions / Cleanup: 1. Restore the real clock and clear browser storage.
Covered Acceptance Criteria:
AC-20, AC-21
Given a session that expires while the landing screen is open, when the landing address is requested again, then liveness is evaluated afresh and the user is taken to /login with the session-expired notice.
Traceability:
Requirement IDs: AC-20, AC-21, FR-14, FR-15, DO2, N3

Test Case Title: Verify that the session is written from exactly one place after a success
Test Case Objective / Description: A second place that writes the session is a second chance to write one that was never authenticated. This test reads the source for every write of the session and confirms there is exactly one, sitting inside the branch reached only when a successful sign-in response has been parsed and accepted.
Preconditions: 1. A checkout of the browser client repository is available.
Test Data:
Scan root = the client repository source tree
Expected number of write call sites = exactly 1
Permitted location = the success branch of the sign-in submission, after the response has been parsed and accepted
Forbidden writers = the landing screen, the route guard, the logout control, the root-address resolver and any helper shipped in production code

contract:
  method: n/a — static source review, no HTTP request is issued
  path: the session store and every module that imports it
  assertion: the session write has exactly one call site and it sits in the parsed-success branch of the sign-in submission
  expected_result: exactly one call site in the permitted location and zero writes from any other module

Automation hint: enforce this with an architecture test that counts imports of the session write and fails above one.
Test Steps:
1. Check out the client repository at the branch under test.
2. Find every module that imports the session write.
3. Count the call sites of the session write across the whole source tree.
4. Read the single call site and the branch it sits inside.
5. Confirm that no landing, guard, logout or root-address module writes the session at all.
Expected Result per Step:
1. The checkout completes and the source tree is present.
2. Exactly one module imports the session write.
3. Exactly one call site exists; no helper and no fallback path adds a second.
4. The call site sits inside the branch reached only after a successful response has been parsed and accepted, so no other state can reach it.
5. Zero writes originate outside the sign-in submission, so nothing after sign-in can create, replace or mutate the stored session.
Expected Outcome: The session can be written from exactly one place, reachable only by a parsed and accepted successful sign-in, so no later screen can create or alter a session.
Postconditions / Cleanup: 1. None — read-only test.
Covered Acceptance Criteria:
AC-8, AC-12
Given the client source, when every write of the session is reviewed, then exactly one call site exists and it sits in the branch reached only by a parsed successful sign-in response.

Requirement IDs: AC-8, AC-12, FR-7, FR-8, DO1, DO2, N3
